The '''2022 Bolton Metropolitan Borough Council election''' took place on 5 May 2022. One third of councillors—20 out of 60—were to be elected. The election took place alongside [[2022 United Kingdom local elections|other local elections across the United Kingdom]].

In the [[2021 Bolton Metropolitan Borough Council election|previous council election in 2021]], the council remained under [[no overall control]]. The [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservatives]] continued running a minority administration with a [[confidence and supply]] arrangement with smaller parties, as they had done prior to the election. [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour]] formed the main opposition with nineteen seats to the Conservatives' twenty.

== Background ==
[[File:Bolton UK local election 2018 map.svg|thumb|Result of the council election when these seats were last contested in 2018]]
[[File:Bolton UK local election 2021 map.svg|thumb|Result of the most recent council election in 2021]]
The [[Local Government Act 1972]] created a two-tier system of metropolitan counties and districts covering [[Greater Manchester]], [[Merseyside]], [[South Yorkshire]], [[Tyne and Wear]], the [[West Midlands (county)|West Midlands]], and [[West Yorkshire]] starting in 1974. Bolton was a district of the Greater Manchester metropolitan county.<ref name=guide>{{cite book |title=Local Government in England and Wales: A Guide to the New System |year=1974 |publisher=[[HMSO]] |location=London |isbn=0-11-750847-0 |page=7 }}</ref> The [[Local Government Act 1985]] abolished the metropolitan counties, with metropolitan districts taking on most of their powers as [[metropolitan borough]]s. The [[Greater Manchester Combined Authority]] was created in 2011 and began electing the [[mayor of Greater Manchester]] from 2017, which was given strategic powers covering a region coterminous with the former Greater Manchester metropolitan county.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2011/908/made |title=The Greater Manchester Combined Authority Order 2011 |publisher=Legislation.gov.uk |access-date=2015-09-07}}</ref>

Since its formation, Bolton Council has variously been under [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour]] control, [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservative]] control and [[no overall control]]. Labour most recently regained its majority in the [[2011 Bolton Metropolitan Borough Council election|2011 council election]], which it held until the [[2019 Bolton Metropolitan Borough Council election|2019 election]]. After the 2019 election, Labour held 23 seats with the Conservatives on 20, the [[Liberal Democrats (UK)|Liberal Democrats]] on 6, the local party [[Farnworth and Kearsley First]] on five, the [[UK Independence Party]] on three and the local party [[Horwich and Blackrod First]] on two, as well as one [[independent politician|independent councillor]]. The Conservatives formed a [[confidence and supply]] agreement with the Liberal Democrats, Farnworth and Kearley First, Horwich and Blackrod First and the UK Independence Party so that they could form a minority administration.<ref>{{Cite web|title='We are not in coalition': Conservatives officially take control of the council|url=https://www.theboltonnews.co.uk/news/17659746.conservatives-officially-take-control-bolton-council/|access-date=2022-01-22|website=The Bolton News|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=Dobson|first=Charlotte|date=2019-05-10|title=Bolton Tories take over council for first time in 40 years|url=https://www.manchestereveningnews.co.uk/news/greater-manchester-news/bolton-council-16257017|access-date=2022-01-22|website=Manchester Evening News|language=en}}</ref> In the [[2021 Bolton Metropolitan Borough Council election|most recent election in 2021]], the Conservatives became the largest party with 20 seats to Labour's nineteen, with seven independents, the Liberal Democrats and Farnworth and Kearsley First on five seats each, Horwich and Blackrod First on five and a single [[UK Independence Party]] councillor remaining. The Conservatives continued to run a minority administration with support from smaller parties.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Tories become largest party after tense Bolton Council election|url=https://www.theboltonnews.co.uk/news/19288166.tories-remain-largest-party-tense-borough-polls/|access-date=2022-01-22|website=The Bolton News|language=en}}</ref> The Liberal Democrats ended their working arrangement with the Conservatives in January 2021.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Double body blow for Bolton's ruling Conservatives as two councillors quit party and Liberal Democrats end working arrangement|url=https://www.theboltonnews.co.uk/news/19011337.double-body-blow-boltons-ruling-conservatives-two-councillors-quit-party-liberal-democrats-end-working-arrangement/|access-date=2022-01-22|website=The Bolton News|language=en}}</ref> Marie Brady, the leader of the Horwich and Blackrod First party, defected to the Conservative Party after the two other councillors from her party voted against the Conservative budget.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Gee |first=Chris |date=2022-03-25 |title=Councillor and leader of Bolton hyperlocal party defects to join Conservatives |url=https://www.manchestereveningnews.co.uk/news/greater-manchester-news/councillor-leader-bolton-hyperlocal-party-23499710 |access-date=2022-03-26 |website=Manchester Evening News |language=en}}</ref>

{{anchor|Bolton For Change}}
The positions up for election in 2022 were last [[2018 Bolton Metropolitan Borough Council election|elected in 2018]]. In that election, the Conservatives won nine seats, Labour won eight, and the Liberal Democrats and Farnworth and Kealey First won two each.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Council |first=Bolton |title=Local Election Results 2018 |url=https://www.bolton.gov.uk/news/article/293/local-election-results-2018 |access-date=2022-03-28 |website=Bolton Council |language=en}}</ref> Prior to this election, [[Reform UK]] formed an electoral pact with newly-formed local party Bolton For Change, running joint candidates under the banner of both parties. This arrangement has continued to the present, with candidates standing for 'Reform UK and Bolton For Change' in 2022, [[2023 Bolton Metropolitan Borough Council election|2023]] and [[2024 Bolton Metropolitan Borough Council election|2024]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Gannon |first=Paul |date=2021-11-21 |title=Reform UK and Bolton For Change |url=https://www.boltonforchange.org/post/bolton-for-change-reform-uk |access-date=2024-07-31 |website=Bolton For Change |language=en}}</ref>

== Electoral process ==

The council elects its councillors in thirds, with a third being up for election every year for three years, with no election in the fourth year.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.gov.uk/guidance/local-government-structure-and-elections#electoral-cycles|title=Local government structure and elections|work=GOV.UK|access-date=2018-04-27|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/694598/Election_Timetable_in_England.pdf|title=Election Timetable in England}}</ref> The election will take place by [[first-past-the-post voting]], with wards generally being represented by three councillors, with one elected in each election year to serve a four-year term.

All [[Elections in the United Kingdom#Registration procedure|registered electors]] ([[British citizen|British]], [[Irish citizen|Irish]], [[Commonwealth citizen|Commonwealth]] and [[European Union]] citizens) living in Bolton aged 18 or over will be entitled to vote in the election. People who live at two addresses in different councils, such as university students with different term-time and holiday addresses, are entitled to be registered for and vote in elections in both local authorities. Voting in-person at polling stations will take place from 07:00 to 22:00 on election day, and voters will be able to apply for postal votes or proxy votes in advance of the election.

== Campaign ==
The Conservative councillor Adele Warren said that increases in the [[cost of living]] would affect the election, with people "frightened about turning their electricity or heating on". She said that the Conservative [[Chancellor of the Exchequer]] [[Rishi Sunak]] "could have gone much, much further" with measures to help people.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-03-25 |title=Tory leaders confident of gains in May local elections |url=https://www.theguardian.com/politics/2022/mar/25/tory-leaders-confident-of-gains-in-may-local-elections |access-date=2022-03-28 |website=The Guardian |language=en}}</ref>
